A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TheoremExplainAgent work. Their main texts, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocations, and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation experiments on 240 theorems, automated quality scores, human-metric correlations, and error analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds retry experiments, text-to-video comparisons, and human interpretability, preference, and educational-feedback studies.

M1.justification: The planner-and-coder pipeline, Manim generation, optional agentic RAG, narration, and five-attempt correction limit remain unchanged. The retry ablation tests the existing procedure; Appendix D discloses implementation details without establishing a method revision.

E1.justification: The 240-theorem benchmark, four STEM disciplines, and three difficulty levels are retained. v2 modestly extends coverage to human error detection and classroom-use feedback, including university teachers alongside students. The text-to-video comparison samples 20 existing benchmark theorems rather than adding subject coverage.

E2.justification: Section 4.5 adds actual comparisons against LTXVideo and Veo2 on 20 theorems, with outputs displayed in Figure 6. This introduces a distinct comparator family beyond the retained LLM-agent configurations and human-made videos. The new preference study uses existing model candidates.

E3.justification: v2 adds retry budgets N=0 through 5, a 20-theorem text-to-video prompting protocol, a 15-person text-then-video correctness study, blinded rankings by 18 annotators on three topics, and educational ratings from 15 students and eight teachers on two topics. The original benchmark and metric-validation protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new retry ablation tests dependence on code-correction opportunities. Section 4.2 adds quantitative human error-detection evidence to the retained chain-code example, while Appendices C and F examine model preferences and perceived educational usefulness. Earlier error categories and gallery case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Table 7 newly reports standard deviations for participant clarity and engagement ratings. Section 6 first supplies correlation p-values of 0.001 and 0.03 for Visual Relevance and Element Layout. Existing Spearman and inter-rater reporting is retained; retry counts are not independent statistical repetitions.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark, correlation, and cost values are unchanged. Added findings include retry-success trajectories, 9/15 participants detecting a flaw after video exposure, intuitiveness ratings of 3.3 versus 3.9, Gemini leading preference rankings, educational-feedback scores, and qualitative LTXVideo/Veo2 failures. New Table 3 reports five-retry RAG rates of 73%, 77%, and 73%, differing without explanation from Table 1's 83.8%, 82.5%, and 80.0%; this does not establish a comparable-setting performance decline.

T1.justification: Neither version develops new theoretical results or proofs. Appendix G adds a conceptual explanation of 'agentic'; the retry-success description concerns an empirical evaluation measure, without new mathematical reasoning or formal properties.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claims about long-form agentic video generation, the 240-theorem benchmark, five evaluation metrics, and visual explanations exposing reasoning flaws. The revised title and shortened conclusion preserve their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges weak human alignment as a limitation of several automated metrics and suggests specialized video evaluators. It also interprets retry benefits, direct video-model failures, and human-use findings. Much of the expanded limitations section consolidates visual-layout, retrieval, cost, and coding problems already discussed in v1.

D1.justification: Appendix D substantially expands reproducibility information with Manim and plugin versions, ChromaDB, the text splitter, text-embedding-005, retrieval threshold 0.5, and k=2 documents per query. It also clarifies API computation and rendering requirements. These are newly disclosed details; existing prompts, cost figures, and artifact-release information remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to LTXVideo, Veo 2, VideoScore, ManimML, Manim DSA, and Russell and Norvig. It introduces positioning against direct text-to-video generation and contextualizes evaluation and agent terminology, while retaining the main related-work discussion and novelty framing.

P1.justification: Changes include the more explicit video-based title, localized paragraph rewrites, a shortened conclusion, expanded limitations, and reorganized appendices. Existing interpretability discussion moves into a dedicated subsection. The introduction, related work, method narrative, and prompt wording are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds a time-indexed video-comparison grid in Figure 6 and new retry, preference, and educational-feedback tables numbered 3, 6, and 7. Existing galleries, the annotation interface, runtime table, and prompts are regrouped or relocated, and selected existing table entries gain bold emphasis. The earlier figures are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility and adds initial human evidence for interpretability and perceived educational usefulness, alongside more explicit metric limitations. These gains are constrained by the interpretability study's fixed text-first order, small study coverage, and the unexplained RAG discrepancy between Tables 1 and 3. The additions make the paper more informative, but do not establish a substantial improvement in evidential reliability.
